Lab 7: Measuring Ideology Without Reading a Single Bill

84-355 Democracy’s Data | Week 7

Your name here

August 05, 2026

Before we start

Here is a hard problem. You want to know how liberal or conservative a member of Congress is. You could read every bill they voted on and score it — but that means you are deciding what counts as liberal, and somebody will reasonably disagree with every call you make.

DW-NOMINATE solves this by refusing to look at the bills at all.

It takes nothing but the pattern of who voted with whom, across every roll call in American history, and asks: what arrangement of members on a line best predicts those votes? The answer falls out of the arithmetic. Nobody read a bill. Nobody labelled a policy. And the line it produces turns out to be the one we call left and right.

Today you will use it to watch Congress come apart.

Everything is base R. Work in order.

Part 1: A scale nobody designed

nom <- read.csv("data/nominate_members.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
dim(nom)
#> [1] 38643     9
head(nom[, c("congress","year","chamber","state","bioname","party","dim1")], 4)
#>   congress year chamber state                  bioname      party  dim1
#> 1       46 1879   House    PA             WHITE, Harry Republican 0.700
#> 2       46 1879   House    NY       PIERCE, Ray Vaughn Republican 0.650
#> 3       46 1879   House    ME    REED, Thomas Brackett Republican 0.571
#> 4       46 1879   House    IA THOMPSON, William George Republican 0.535

Every member of the House and Senate since 1879. dim1 is the left–right coordinate: negative is liberal, positive is conservative, and the scale runs roughly −1 to +1.

Look at the current House:

now <- max(nom$congress)
h <- nom[nom$chamber == "House", ]
cur <- h[h$congress == now, ]

c(congress = now, year = cur$year[1], members = nrow(cur))
#> congress     year  members 
#>      119     2025      449
aggregate(dim1 ~ party, data = cur, FUN = function(x) round(median(x), 3))
#>        party   dim1
#> 1   Democrat -0.396
#> 2 Republican  0.530
par(mar = c(4, 1, 3, 1))
plot(cur$dim1, jitter(rep(1, nrow(cur)), 8), pch = 19, cex = 0.7,
     col = ifelse(cur$party == "Democrat", "#2166AC66", "#B2182B66"),
     yaxt = "n", ylab = "", xlab = "DW-NOMINATE dimension 1 (liberal → conservative)",
     xlim = c(-1, 1), main = paste0("The House, ", cur$year[1]))
abline(v = 0, lty = 3, col = "grey60")

Two clouds, and nothing between them. That separation is not something anybody put into the method — it is what the voting produced.

Part 2: It was not always like this

The same picture, sixty years earlier.

par(mfrow = c(3, 1), mar = c(3.5, 1, 2.5, 1))
for (cg in c(90, 105, now)) {
  x <- h[h$congress == cg, ]
  plot(x$dim1, jitter(rep(1, nrow(x)), 8), pch = 19, cex = 0.7,
       col = ifelse(x$party == "Democrat", "#2166AC66", "#B2182B66"),
       yaxt = "n", ylab = "", xlab = "", xlim = c(-1, 1),
       main = paste0(cg, "th Congress (", x$year[1], ")"))
  abline(v = 0, lty = 3, col = "grey60")
}

par(mfrow = c(1, 1))

In 1967 the two clouds overlap in the middle. There were liberal Republicans and conservative Democrats, and they sat in the same ideological space.

Part 3: The gap, measured

Take the median of each party in each Congress and subtract.

med <- function(cg, p) median(h$dim1[h$congress == cg & h$party == p])
cgs <- sort(unique(h$congress))

gap <- data.frame(
  congress = cgs,
  year = 1789 + 2 * (cgs - 1),
  dem  = sapply(cgs, med, p = "Democrat"),
  rep  = sapply(cgs, med, p = "Republican"))
gap$gap <- gap$rep - gap$dem

tail(gap, 4)
#>    congress year     dem    rep    gap
#> 71      116 2019 -0.3805 0.5045 0.8850
#> 72      117 2021 -0.3850 0.4980 0.8830
#> 73      118 2023 -0.3890 0.5040 0.8930
#> 74      119 2025 -0.3955 0.5300 0.9255
plot(gap$year, gap$gap, type = "l", lwd = 2.5, col = "#54278F",
     xlab = "", ylab = "Distance between party medians",
     main = "How far apart the two parties are, House, 1879-present")
abline(h = 0, col = "grey70")

gap[gap$congress %in% c(90, 100, 110, now), c("congress","year","dem","rep","gap")]
#>    congress year     dem   rep    gap
#> 45       90 1967 -0.3425 0.241 0.5835
#> 55      100 1987 -0.3200 0.346 0.6660
#> 65      110 2007 -0.3790 0.426 0.8050
#> 74      119 2025 -0.3955 0.530 0.9255

The gap was 0.584 in 1967. It is 0.925 now — the widest in this entire series, which reaches back to 1879.

But look at the left half of that plot before you conclude anything. The 1890s reached 0.852, not far below today. The genuine outlier is the middle of the twentieth century: the narrowest gap on record is 0.498, in 1947. The shape is a U, and the era that produced most of our intuitions about how Congress is supposed to work sits at the bottom of it.

Part 4: The overlap, and the year it ran out

A sharper question than “how far apart are the medians?” is: is there anybody in between?

Count the Republicans who sit to the left of the most conservative Democrat.

overlap <- function(cg) {
  x <- h[h$congress == cg, ]
  sum(x$dim1[x$party == "Republican"] < max(x$dim1[x$party == "Democrat"]))
}
ov <- data.frame(congress = cgs, year = gap$year,
                 overlapping = sapply(cgs, overlap))

ov[ov$congress %in% 100:112, ]
#>    congress year overlapping
#> 55      100 1987          26
#> 56      101 1989          11
#> 57      102 1991           9
#> 58      103 1993           5
#> 59      104 1995           3
#> 60      105 1997           5
#> 61      106 1999           4
#> 62      107 2001           2
#> 63      108 2003           0
#> 64      109 2005           0
#> 65      110 2007           0
#> 66      111 2009           0
#> 67      112 2011           0
plot(ov$year, ov$overlapping, type = "h", lwd = 2, col = "#B2182B",
     xlab = "", ylab = "Republicans left of the rightmost Democrat",
     main = "The vanishing middle")

The 107th Congress — 2001 to 2002 — was the last one in which a single Republican sat to the left of a single Democrat. There were two of them. Since the 108th, in 2003, the number has been zero every time.

Part 5: Both parties moved. They did not move equally.

c(dem_1967 = round(med(90, "Democrat"), 3),
  dem_now  = round(med(now, "Democrat"), 3),
  dem_moved = round(med(now, "Democrat") - med(90, "Democrat"), 3))
#>  dem_1967   dem_now dem_moved 
#>    -0.342    -0.396    -0.053
c(rep_1967 = round(med(90, "Republican"), 3),
  rep_now  = round(med(now, "Republican"), 3),
  rep_moved = round(med(now, "Republican") - med(90, "Republican"), 3))
#>  rep_1967   rep_now rep_moved 
#>     0.241     0.530     0.289
plot(gap$year, gap$rep, type = "l", lwd = 2.5, col = "#B2182B",
     ylim = c(-0.6, 0.7), xlab = "", ylab = "Party median, dimension 1",
     main = "Each party's median over time")
lines(gap$year, gap$dem, lwd = 2.5, col = "#2166AC")
abline(h = 0, col = "grey70", lty = 3)
legend("topleft", c("Republicans", "Democrats"),
       col = c("#B2182B", "#2166AC"), lwd = 2.5, bty = "n")

Since 1967 the Democratic median has moved 0.053 to the left. The Republican median has moved 0.289 to the right — five and a half times as far.

This is the finding called asymmetric polarization, and it is one of the most contested claims in the study of Congress. Part 6 is about why.

Part 6: What the number cannot tell you

The scale is relative, not absolute. DW-NOMINATE places members relative to the votes actually held. If Congress stops voting on some issues and starts voting on others, a member who never changed her mind can move on the scale. “Republicans moved right” and “the agenda moved and Republicans stayed put” produce the same picture here, and this data cannot separate them. That is the serious objection to the asymmetry finding, and you should take it seriously.

It measures voting, not belief. A member who votes with her party while privately disagreeing looks identical to a true believer.

And it is elites, not voters. Everything here is about 535 people. Whether the public has polarized the same way is a different question with different data — which is exactly the debate we set up on Tuesday.

sapply(c(80, 90, 100, now), function(cg) round(sd(h$dim2[h$congress == cg]), 3))
#> [1] 0.561 0.487 0.406 0.315

One more thing the method knows: there is a second dimension, and it used to matter. It captured the split over civil rights that cut across both parties. Its spread has fallen from 0.561 in 1947 to 0.315 today. American politics used to be two-dimensional. It is now very nearly one.

Part 7: On your own

This is the part you turn in. You are not being asked to write code. Each option is a working chunk with one thing to change.

Pick one.

Option A — The Senate, or another era

which_chamber <- "Senate"        # <- change to "House"

ch <- nom[nom$chamber == which_chamber, ]
cg2 <- sort(unique(ch$congress))
m2 <- function(cg, p) median(ch$dim1[ch$congress == cg & ch$party == p])
g2 <- data.frame(year = 1789 + 2*(cg2-1),
                 dem = sapply(cg2, m2, p = "Democrat"),
                 rep = sapply(cg2, m2, p = "Republican"))
g2$gap <- g2$rep - g2$dem

plot(g2$year, g2$gap, type = "l", lwd = 2.5, col = "#54278F",
     xlab = "", ylab = "Distance between party medians",
     main = paste("Party distance,", which_chamber))

g2[g2$year %in% c(1967, 1987, 2007, max(g2$year)), ]
#>    year     dem    rep    gap
#> 45 1967 -0.3120 0.2750 0.5870
#> 55 1987 -0.3130 0.3025 0.6155
#> 65 2007 -0.3135 0.3950 0.7085
#> 74 2025 -0.3560 0.5615 0.9175

Write about: does the Senate tell the same story as the House? Report the 1967 gap and the current one for your chamber. The Senate is smaller, its members serve six years, and its states are whole states rather than drawn districts — if districting were the main driver of polarization, the Senate should look different. Does it? What does your answer imply about the gerrymandering explanation you will meet in Week 15?

Option B — Has this happened before?

start_year <- 1879              # <- change this. Try 1930, 1950, 1980.

g <- gap[gap$year >= start_year, ]
plot(g$year, g$gap, type = "l", lwd = 2.5, col = "#54278F",
     xlab = "", ylab = "Distance between party medians",
     main = paste("Party distance from", start_year))
abline(h = gap$gap[gap$congress == 90], lty = 2, col = "grey50")

# The most and least polarized Congresses on record
rbind(head(gap[order(-gap$gap), c("congress","year","gap")], 4),
      head(gap[order( gap$gap), c("congress","year","gap")], 4))
#>    congress year    gap
#> 74      119 2025 0.9255
#> 73      118 2023 0.8930
#> 70      115 2017 0.8890
#> 69      114 2015 0.8860
#> 35       80 1947 0.4975
#> 33       78 1943 0.5320
#> 31       76 1939 0.5345
#> 38       83 1953 0.5455
# Congresses with no overlap at all
ov$year[ov$overlapping == 0]
#>  [1] 1879 1881 1883 1889 1891 1893 1897 1899 1901 1903 1905 1907 1911 1913 1915
#> [16] 1917 1919 2003 2005 2007 2009 2011 2013 2015 2017 2019 2021 2023 2025

Write about: start at 1980 and the story is a straight line upward. Start at 1879 and it is a U. Which is the honest picture? Note that zero overlap is not new — it also happened repeatedly between 1879 and 1921. Then the harder question: if the mid-twentieth century was the unusual period rather than the current one, what does that do to the way polarization is usually discussed?

Option C — Who is in the middle?

which_congress <- 90            # <- change this. Try 100, 107, 119.

x <- h[h$congress == which_congress, ]
dmax <- max(x$dim1[x$party == "Democrat"])
dmin <- min(x$dim1[x$party == "Republican"])

cat("Congress", which_congress, "(", x$year[1], ")\n")
#> Congress 90 ( 1967 )
cat("most conservative Democrat: ", round(dmax, 3), "\n")
#> most conservative Democrat:  0.333
cat("most liberal Republican:    ", round(dmin, 3), "\n")
#> most liberal Republican:     -0.139
cat("members in the overlap:     ", sum(x$dim1 > dmin & x$dim1 < dmax), "\n\n")
#> members in the overlap:      204
mid <- x[x$dim1 > dmin & x$dim1 < dmax, c("bioname","party","state","dim1")]
head(mid[order(mid$dim1), ], 12)
#>                                  bioname      party state   dim1
#> 22540            WHITE, Richard Crawford   Democrat    TX -0.137
#> 22539          LANDRUM, Phillip Mitchell   Democrat    GA -0.134
#> 22538               ROBERTS, Herbert Ray   Democrat    TX -0.131
#> 22536           SIKES, Robert Lee Fulton   Democrat    FL -0.128
#> 22537              JONES, Paul Caruthers   Democrat    MO -0.128
#> 22535           GETTYS, Thomas Smithwick   Democrat    SC -0.122
#> 22534 STUCKEY, Williamson Sylvester, Jr.   Democrat    GA -0.114
#> 22533         HULL, William Raleigh, Jr.   Democrat    MO -0.112
#> 22532            HENDERSON, David Newton   Democrat    NC -0.108
#> 22531                  TEAGUE, Olin Earl   Democrat    TX -0.102
#> 22530             CASEY, Robert Randolph   Democrat    TX -0.098
#> 22529                   HALPERN, Seymour Republican    NY -0.094

Write about: who were these people, and where were they from? Run it for the 90th and you will get a long list; run it for the 107th and you will get almost nobody. Look at the states in the 90th — the conservative Democrats and the liberal Republicans were not randomly scattered. Connect that to Week 4’s Solid South: what happened to those members, and was it that they changed their minds or that they were replaced?

Option D — Ask your own question

Look up a member you have heard of. Compare your own state’s delegation across two eras. Follow whatever nags.

What to submit. Knit to HTML or PDF and upload to Canvas, with your chosen chunk and two or three paragraphs of interpretation.

The writing is the assignment. I am not grading your code — it is my code. I am grading whether you can read a measurement carefully enough to say what it does and does not establish.

Where the data came from

Voteview (https://voteview.com) — Jeffrey B. Lewis, Keith Poole, Howard Rosenthal, Adam Boche, Aaron Rudkin and Luke Sonnet, Congressional Roll-Call Votes Database. Every member of the House and Senate from the 46th Congress (1879) to the present, with DW-NOMINATE coordinates.

Three things about this file worth holding on to:

  • Presidents are in the source and are dropped here. They receive scores based on announced positions rather than roll calls, and folding them into a chamber median would compare unlike things.
  • The current Congress is still voting. Its scores are estimated from the roll calls held so far and will shift slightly.
  • The scale is estimated, not observed. DW-NOMINATE is a model fitted to votes; the coordinates have uncertainty that this file does not carry, and small differences between two members are not meaningful.

The script that downloaded, filtered and checked the file is data/build-data.R. It prints the party medians, the asymmetry, and the overlap series, so the numbers in this lab can be checked against the source in one command.
